messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Authority Presence: Police, Known People: Related people, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajesh is a forty-nine-year-old married man who works as a military medic. He came to therapy reluctantly, at his wife’s urging, after months of what he described as “just not being myself.” What emerged slowly over the first two sessions was a story he had never told anyone, not even his wife, because he could not find the words for it. The event itself happened three years ago, when he was still living with his partner at the time—a relationship he had believed was stable and loving. One evening, after a minor disagreement about money, she turned on him with a violence that felt both sudden and, in retrospect, eerily inevitable. She struck him repeatedly across the face and body, kicked him while he was on the ground, and screamed at him in a voice he still hears sometimes when he is trying to fall asleep. He did not fight back. He was a medic, trained to de-escalate, trained to protect others, and he froze. What stayed with him most vividly was not the visual image of her face but the physical sensation of the blows—the sharp pain in his ribs, the aching throb in his jaw that lasted for weeks. When the memory returns now, he feels that same pain again, exactly where it was, as if the bruising has never fully healed.

In the months after the assault, Rajesh tried to go on as normal. He continued his work at the base clinic, treating soldiers with combat injuries and routine illnesses. But something had shifted in how he moved through the world. He began to notice that he could not stand the smell of sweat or body odour—the particular, intimate scent of another person’s exertion. It would hit him in the gym, in the crowded break room, even in the exam room when a patient came in after a long patrol. His stomach would clench, his heart would pound, and he would feel the old pain in his ribs as if she were standing over him again. He stopped going to the gym altogether, telling himself he was too tired. He started avoiding people whenever he could—eating lunch alone in his office, taking the long way around the hospital corridor to avoid the waiting area. When he had to treat a patient, he would keep the encounter as brief and impersonal as possible, cutting off conversation, stepping back from the bed. He had come to believe that there was something fundamentally wrong with him as a person, that he had been weak for not defending himself, that he had somehow deserved what happened because he had not seen it coming.

The consequences accumulated quietly. His wife noticed that he no longer wanted to go out to dinner or to visit her family. He would make excuses—work was exhausting, he had a headache—and she stopped pressing. At night, he lay awake for hours, his body tense, his ears straining for any sound that might signal danger. Ordinary noises—the creak of the house settling, the hum of the refrigerator, a car door closing down the street—made him jump, his heart hammering before his mind could catch up. He felt safe only in the bedroom with the door locked, and even then, he would check the window twice before lying down. During the day, he found himself avoiding certain clothes—anything that resembled the shirt he had been wearing that night, a dark blue polo. He threw it away but could not bring himself to buy another one in that colour.

What frightened Rajesh most was not the memories themselves but the way they took over. When a flashback came—triggered by a police car he passed on the road, or by the sight of a colleague whose build reminded him of his ex-partner—he felt as though he was back in that apartment, reliving it moment by moment. He could not describe the event in words, not even to himself. The story felt stuck in his body, in the ache of his ribs and the tightness in his jaw. He had stopped believing that anything in his life had meaning. His work, which had once felt like a calling, now seemed hollow. The people who had hurt him—his ex-partner—had faced no consequences. She had moved on, and he was the one still trapped.

He came to therapy because his wife told him she could not watch him disappear anymore. What he hopes for, though he cannot quite say it, is to feel like the person he was before—the medic who could walk into any room and know what to do. What he fears is that that person is gone for good, and that the pain in his ribs will never really stop.
